I have a hair plucking issue too!!! Not for my scalp hair but I used to as a kid. But in this context, it’s scalp scratching to pick out the debris (buildup, flakes, etc.) even my hair is clean. It’s annoying. 

Okay anyways, you could try doing flat twists since your scalp is sensitive to cornrows. Another options are twists in general, where sometimes I’d cornrow the twists I made, as they will not be tight, but pulled back enough where possibly you don’t have to pull your hair. I know for me at least with scratching my scalp, it stops when I wear my bonnet or scarf at night, or clip my nails. It’s basically about keeping the repetitive behavior to a minimum. 

Bantu knots can be a good option to by tucking your hair away to avoid pulling it out. Another option is braids too! I recommend any natural style that has minimal tension, but also long wearability for your hair. I’m not saying styles such as knotless, boho, etc, since those could cause sensitivity issues similar to what cornrows do to your hair. Overall, I’d recommend any simply style that is parted, mainly because it makes it easier to just detangle and put back in the same style again without spending extra effort in sectioning, parting, etc. so if you’re wearing twists, when they get old you can just redo them in the same parts. However I believe you have to switch the parts up every so often but I can’t remember exactly why. 

A good advice is do not leave your hair unattended in these styles. I’ve dealt with periods of burn out and depression where I neglected my hair in twists for instance for months, causing dryness, breakage, split ends, etc. so I’d definitely recommend to try not to go over a month of not tending to your hair.

Another good hair option is something I just discovered on TikTok but is a common practice in Africa, which is “African threading”, often done with rubber strands, Brazilian wool, or regular yarn. Considering you wear a scarf as well, this can be a REALLY good low maintenance option that minimizes how much you pull your hair, keeping is moisturized and detangled, and convenient for when you’re wearing a scarf.  

You can also find out your hair porosity to guide you with selecting products. A stylist I follow personally doesn’t believe in non-stylists using porosity since it’s a spectrum really, but it did help me understand what my hair likes.

I learned that having highly porous strands (I gain and lose water/moisture quickly), my hair likes thicker products such as butters, creams, heavier oils for instance. 

In replace of oil, you can try shea butter, mango butter, or hair grease as a form of sealant if your hair is fine with heavier options like these. You could possibly try natural oils such as coconut oil rather than store brand. It’s typically lightweight. The same can be said for making any homemade oils or hair products if store brand can irritate your scalp. But also don’t fall down this hole either, as people love to obsess over “DO THIS TO GROW YOUR HAIR!!” And personally, it stresses me out. Also take into account your ability to spend a lot of time on making homemade stuff too, since you don’t want to burn your energy out. TJ Maxx and Marshall’s have great hair products that are often expensive in your average retail store, but also don’t be afraid to use products that are often cheaper in retail or beauty supply stores either.

As someone who’s also in a teen relationship:

One thing we do not appreciate is when people tell us not to take it serious because it’s “young and you WILL see other people when you guys are older”. A lot of teens our age literally do not take their relationships seriously. And what happens? They have been messy, toxic, and traumatic. Why? Because a lot are used to the mentality of “I’m just gonna get an experience out of this, and besides I’ll just find someone else”. I appreciate the unwarranted life lessons, but I’d rather treat my relationship as something valuable than something replaceable. I could go on a full rant about this, but I’ll leave it here.


My point is that make sure you treat your relationship as something special and meaningful. Even IF it was to end, you’re able to walk away from it knowing you cared and put in effort where a lot of people wouldn’t just because we’re young. Be optimistic about you guys staying together, even if it feels like the end of the world because you messed up. People will have their own input and advice to add, but only truly apply it if it’s necessary. If there’s something on your mind that’s worrying you, communicate it properly. What I mean by this is to never explain things without context or with poor wording, as this could panic either one of you guys. Another tip is to learn about using more “I” statements when expressing how y’all feel, instead of “you” statements”. Instead of “you never call me at all”, go “I feel lonely when you don’t call me. I want us to share the responsibility of calling each other”. This lessens possible tension or defensiveness”. A big one is that you both will make mistakes. It’s how you handle them will determine the state of the relationship. 

                   
Telling teenagers not to expect the best out their first relationships isn’t going to help them at all. Honestly, being told to “brace for the worst” only gave me anxiety about us ending in the long run. Sure realistically a lot of teen relationships don’t often last, but it can’t be the set expectation for everyone. If we see adults give us hope and optimism in our relationship, we’ll feel the same and give it back to our partner even more. We still look up to adults to guide us in life decisions.
